La <strong>dinámica de sistemas</strong>: System dynamics is the art of describing the world with baths: a country's population, the money in an account, the CO₂ in the atmosphere, the sick in an epidemic, the stock in a warehouse. A few stocks, the flows connecting them and the [[cib-realimentacion|feedback]] loops that make the flows depend on the stocks are enough to explain surprising behaviour: growth that stops suddenly, oscillations nobody is looking for and collapses nobody sees coming.

La dinámica de sistemas nació en 1956, c: System dynamics was born in 1956, when Jay Forrester, an MIT engineer who had invented the magnetic core memory of the first computers, moved to the business school and began simulating firms as if they were circuits. In 1972, a team trained in his group published The Limits to Growth, a report for the Club of Rome that simulated by computer the population, the resources and the pollution of the planet. Its principal author was Donella Meadows, a doctor of biophysics, who devoted the rest of her life to teaching people to think in systems. Her essay on “leverage points”, the places where a small change transforms a whole system, is still a standard read. And it was another woman, Elinor Ostrom, who proved by studying fisheries and irrigation systems all over the world that the tragedy of the commons is not inevitable: many communities give themselves rules that avoid it. For that she received in 2009 the Nobel Prize in Economics, the first woman to do so.
